titulo: Scenario 5 — Claude Code for Continuous Integration

questoes.pergunta:
Orbital Logística runs Claude Code in the GitHub Actions pipelines of its monorepo to review pull requests and generate tests.

The first review job was written as `claude "Review this PR's diff and list problems"`. The job hangs until it hits the 60-minute timeout, without producing any output. What is the fix?
opcoes: Increase the job timeout to 120 minutes, because large diffs take a long time to analyze.
Run in non-interactive mode with `-p` (`--print`), which processes the prompt, prints the result, and exits.
Add `--permission-mode bypassPermissions`, so the agent never stops waiting for tool approval during the job.
Pipe `yes |` before the command, automatically answering any interactive question.
questoes.explicacao: Without `-p`, Claude Code opens the interactive session and waits for input indefinitely. `-p` is the primitive for use in scripts and CI.
feedbacks: Treats the symptom: in interactive mode the process will never finish on its own, whatever the timeout.
Correct: the process hangs because it's in interactive mode; `-p` solves it.
Tempting because permission prompts also hang, but the session would remain interactive; besides, bypass isn't the right posture for CI.
A hack that doesn't make the session non-interactive and may approve unwanted actions.

questoes.pergunta:
At Orbital Logística, the Claude Code review job runs with `-p`, and the next pipeline step posts each finding as a line comment on the PR.

Today that step extracts the findings from free text with regular expressions and breaks whenever the wording changes. What is the best solution?
opcoes: Reinforce in the prompt: "respond ONLY with valid JSON, with no text before or after".
Switch to `--output-format stream-json`, which already delivers each finding as a separate object.
Use `--output-format json` with `--json-schema` describing the findings and consume the validated JSON.
Add a second call to Claude that converts the first call's free text into JSON before the posting step.
questoes.explicacao: For machine consumption, use JSON output with a schema: the result comes back structured and conforming to the format the next step expects.
feedbacks: An improvement, but still probabilistic: a prompt instruction doesn't guarantee format.
`stream-json` emits execution events (messages, tool calls) as a stream; it doesn't structure the review content into the fields the step needs.
Correct: structured output with a schema eliminates fragile parsing.
More cost and one more point of failure to solve something the invocation itself solves with a schema.

questoes.pergunta:
Orbital Logística wants the CI review job to run without human intervention, without hanging on permission requests, without being able to modify the repository, and without running indefinitely.

Which two configurations meet these requirements? (Choose TWO.)
opcoes: A prompt instruction: "do not edit any file and finish as quickly as possible".
`--allowedTools` allowing only the read tools (Read, Grep, Glob) and the project's specific test command.
A GitHub token with administrator permission, so the agent never runs into a lack of access.
`--max-turns` with a limit compatible with the typical size of a review, as a safety ceiling.
`--permission-mode bypassPermissions`, so no tool asks for approval.
questoes.explicacao: In CI, restrict the tools explicitly (least privilege, no permission prompts for what is allowed) and use `--max-turns` as a backstop against endless execution.
feedbacks: A critical rule in the prompt is probabilistic; it doesn't prevent edits or guarantee termination.
Correct: allows what's needed without prompts and prevents edits deterministically.
Violates least privilege and widens the possible damage from a wrong action.
Correct: a turn ceiling is a valid backstop (not the primary termination mechanism, which remains the task's natural completion).
Removes the prompts, but also all the controls: the agent could edit or execute anything.

questoes.pergunta:
At Orbital Logística, the review job uses `claude -p --output-format json --max-turns 25`. The next step approves the PR check when the list of findings is empty.

On a very large PR, the run hits the turn limit before finishing and the result comes back with no findings. The check turns green. How should the pipeline handle this case?
opcoes: Search the result text for words like "LGTM" or "approved" to decide the check status.
Automatically rerun with the same limit until it finishes without hitting it, as many times as needed, and only then publish the check status.
Check the status/subtype of the JSON result and, if the run did not finish normally, mark the check as failed or inconclusive, never as approved.
Treat the absence of findings as approval, since the agent analyzed what it could within the limit.
questoes.explicacao: An interrupted run is not an empty success. The pipeline must look at the result's structured status (just as you look at `stop_reason` in a loop) and propagate the failure instead of silencing it.
feedbacks: Deciding termination by reading natural language is an anti-pattern; use the structured status field.
Unbounded retry may never converge on a PR that is too large; the problem calls for explicit handling (and perhaps multi-pass review).
Correct: distinguishes "nothing found" from "didn't finish" and avoids silent approval.
It's the anti-pattern of treating failure as empty: the review simply didn't happen in full.

questoes.pergunta:
Orbital Logística's developers want to mention `@claude` in pull request comments to ask for explanations and small fixes, with minimal in-house infrastructure to maintain.

Which approach best meets this need?
opcoes: Ask each developer to run Claude Code locally and paste the response into the PR.
Build an in-house webhook server that receives GitHub events and calls `claude -p` for each mention, with full control over the flow.
Use the managed GitHub Actions integration (`claude-code-action`), configured in the repository's workflow.
Schedule a job every 10 minutes that reads all new comments and sends a batch to the Batch API.
questoes.explicacao: For the standard case of interacting with PRs/issues on GitHub, the managed integration solves it with less maintenance. `-p` is the primitive when you need full control.
feedbacks: Automates nothing and doesn't meet the request for integration in the PR.
Works, but it's more complex than necessary; it reinvents what the managed integration already offers.
Correct: meets the requirement with the simplest ready-made solution.
The Batch API has a window of up to 24h and isn't meant for interaction; the response to a mention needs to be fast.

questoes.pergunta:
An Orbital Logística pipeline has two steps: a `claude -p` session generates a bug fix and then the same session is resumed with `--resume` and receives the request "now critically review the code you wrote".

The review step almost never flags problems, but humans find several afterward. What is the best change?
opcoes: Increase the review step's `effort`, so the model reasons more deeply about each of the decisions made in the code it just wrote itself.
Do the review in an independent invocation (new session, without the generation history), receiving only the diff and the review criteria.
Run the review twice in a row in the same session and merge the findings.
Keep the same session, but reinforce in the prompt: "be extremely critical and find at least three problems".
questoes.explicacao: Whoever generated the code carries the reasoning context that justified the decisions and tends not to question them. Review must happen in an independent session.
feedbacks: More effort in the same session remains biased by the reasoning that produced the code.
Correct: eliminates the bias from the generation's reasoning context.
Repeating in the same context repeats the same bias.
Forcing a quota of problems generates false positives and doesn't remove the bias of the session that wrote the code.

questoes.pergunta:
Orbital Logística receives refactoring PRs with 40 to 60 files. The current review job passes the entire diff to Claude in a single call.

The reviews of these PRs are inconsistent: some files get detailed analysis, others none, and bugs involving two modules go unnoticed. Which review architecture solves this?
opcoes: Use a model with a larger context window, so the entire diff fits comfortably in a single call.
Add to the prompt: "review all files with the same level of detail and attention to cross-module bugs".
Split the diff into fixed batches of 10 files, review each batch, and concatenate the results.
Multi-pass review: one pass per file with the same local-analysis prompt, followed by an integration pass that receives the findings and examines the interactions between files.
questoes.explicacao: On a large PR, a single pass dilutes attention. The per-file pass ensures consistent local analysis; the integration pass covers data flow and contracts between modules.
feedbacks: Fitting in the window doesn't solve attention dilution; a larger context still suffers from lost in the middle.
An instruction doesn't change the structural limitation of a single call over an enormous diff.
Improves local analysis, but arbitrary batches without an integration pass still miss cross-file bugs.
Correct: addresses both attention dilution and cross-file bugs.

questoes.pergunta:
Orbital Logística implemented multi-pass review: each file in the PR is analyzed in a separate call, and then the integration pass runs.

What should the integration pass receive as input to be effective?
opcoes: The structured findings from the per-file passes and the changes to interfaces and contracts between modules, with the instruction to focus on data flow and errors at the boundaries.
The same prompt as the per-file passes, now applied to all the files together.
Only the full PR diff, without the per-file findings, so the analysis isn't influenced.
Only the PR description written by the author, which summarizes the intent of the change.
questoes.explicacao: The integration pass receives the local findings and focuses on what only shows up between files: data flow, contracts, and error handling at the boundaries.
feedbacks: Correct: gives the integration pass the right material and a different focus from the local passes.
Repeating the local analysis at scale reproduces the single-pass failure; the integration pass needs a different prompt.
Goes back to the original problem: one call over the entire diff, without focus, with diluted attention.
The author's intent is useful as context, but on its own it doesn't make it possible to find bugs in the code.

questoes.pergunta:
Orbital Logística is reviewing its uses of Claude in CI to reduce cost. The Batch API costs 50% less, but processes within up to 24 hours, with no SLA.

Which two workloads are good candidates to migrate to the Batch API? (Choose TWO.)
opcoes: The nightly security audit that analyzes the monorepo's 3,000 files and publishes a report in the morning.
The mandatory review check that blocks the merge until it receives the result.
The agent that fixes broken tests by reading files and running the suite over several rounds.
The interactive debugging of a broken build, done by an on-call developer.
The weekly technical debt report generated from all the modules.
questoes.explicacao: Batch is for bulk work with no urgency (nightly, weekly). It isn't for a blocking step, real-time interaction, or a multi-turn tool loop.
feedbacks: Correct: nightly bulk work tolerates the batch window.
A blocking pre-merge check can't wait up to 24h with no SLA; it needs to be synchronous.
A batch request doesn't support a multi-turn tool loop; this agent needs to run synchronously.
Interactive debugging requires an immediate response.
Correct: a periodic report with no urgency is the typical use case.

questoes.pergunta:
Orbital Logística's nightly audit sends a batch with one request per file. The script that processes the results matches each result to its file by its position in the submitted list.

The morning report has started attributing vulnerabilities to the wrong files. What is the fix?
opcoes: Sort the results by each request's completion time before matching them to the file list, reproducing the original submission order.
Replace the batch with sequential synchronous calls, which preserve order.
Send a separate batch for each file, guaranteeing one-to-one correspondence.
Give each request a `custom_id` that identifies the file (e.g., its path or hash) and match the results by that field.
questoes.explicacao: Batch results may arrive out of submission order. Matching must be done by `custom_id`.
feedbacks: Completion order also has no relation to submission order; the problem remains.
Gives up the 50% discount and the batch's scale to solve a correlation problem.
Works, but creates thousands of batches to work around something `custom_id` solves.
Correct: `custom_id` is the designed mechanism for matching requests and results.

questoes.pergunta:
Orbital Logística's nightly batch has 3,000 requests. In the morning, 2,880 are `succeeded`, 90 are `errored`, and 30 are `expired`.

What is the correct action to complete the audit?
opcoes: Migrate the entire audit to synchronous calls, since the batch has proven unreliable.
Ignore the 120 requests, since 96% coverage is enough for a nightly report.
Resubmit the entire batch, to ensure all results come from the same run.
Resubmit in a new batch only the 120 requests that failed or expired, identified by their `custom_id`, after checking the cause of the errors.
questoes.explicacao: Reprocess only the `custom_id`s that failed; resubmitting everything costs double with no gain. Checking the cause of the errors avoids repeating a validation failure.
feedbacks: A disproportionate reaction: partial failures are expected and handled by selective resubmission.
Silences a gap: unaudited files create a false sense of coverage.
Pays again for 2,880 results that are already done.
Correct: cheap and complete, with diagnosis before resubmission.

questoes.pergunta:
Orbital Logística tried to move to the nightly batch an analysis in which, for each file, Claude calls a tool to read the imported files before concluding.

The results come back with a pending `tool_use` and no conclusion. How should this workload be redesigned for the batch?
opcoes: Pre-collect in code the necessary content (the file and its relevant imports) and send it all in each request, so the analysis finishes in a single response.
Use `tool_choice` to force the model to never call tools inside the batch.
Poll the batch status more frequently to return the tool results in time.
Configure the batch to automatically execute the tools and continue the conversation until `end_turn`.
questoes.explicacao: A batch request doesn't run a multi-turn tool loop. Either the full context goes in the request, or the workload must run as a synchronous agent.
feedbacks: Correct: turns the task into a single-turn one, compatible with the batch.
Preventing the tool doesn't solve it: the model would still lack the imports it needs to conclude.
Polling doesn't allow injecting a `tool_result` into a batch request that has already been processed.
No such client-side tool loop execution exists inside the batch.

questoes.pergunta:
Each Orbital Logística review sends Claude ~30,000 tokens of coding guidelines and tool definitions, followed by the diff. The system prompt starts with `Build #{BUILD_ID} - {timestamp}` and then contains the guidelines, with a `cache_control` breakpoint at their end.

The team expected to save with prompt caching, but `usage.cache_read_input_tokens` is always zero. What is the cause and the fix?
opcoes: The default TTL is too short; switching to the 1-hour cache solves it, since the builds are spaced apart.
The guidelines are too large for the cache; they must be reduced to below the minimum.
A single breakpoint isn't enough for 30,000 tokens; you must use all four available breakpoints.
The ID and timestamp at the start change the prefix on every run; move them after the last breakpoint (or into the user message), leaving the stable content first.
questoes.explicacao: The cache matches the exact prefix (tools → system → messages). Any variable byte before the breakpoint invalidates everything. Stable content first, volatile content after.
feedbacks: With the prefix changing on every build, no TTL helps: the cache never matches.
Inverts the rule: there's a minimum size for caching (below it nothing is cached), not a maximum in this range.
More breakpoints don't fix a prefix that changes right at the start.
Correct: removes the silent invalidator from the prefix.

questoes.pergunta:
After fixing the system prompt, Orbital Logística still sees `cache_read_input_tokens` fluctuating between zero and the expected value in the CI reviews.

Which two pipeline practices may be silently invalidating the cache? (Choose TWO.)
opcoes: The PR diff is placed in the user message, after the cache breakpoint.
The guidelines live in a versioned file and only change when the team updates the coding standard.
The tool definitions are built from a dictionary without stable ordering, and the order varies between runs.
The repository ID and the branch name are interpolated into the system prompt before the guidelines.
The `cache_control` breakpoint is at the end of the guidelines block, which is identical in every run.
questoes.explicacao: Silent invalidators: non-deterministic ordering of tools/keys, variable values (IDs, branch, timestamp) in the prefix, tools that vary per request. Volatile content after the breakpoint doesn't hurt.
feedbacks: That's the right way: volatile content after the breakpoint doesn't invalidate the cached prefix.
An occasional, intentional change creates a new cache; it doesn't explain the fluctuation between runs.
Correct: tools are part of the prefix; a different order is a different prefix.
Correct: values that vary between runs at the start of the system prompt change the prefix.
This is the recommended placement: the breakpoint at the end of the stable content.

questoes.pergunta:
Orbital Logística's automated review classifies findings into four categories: security, bugs, performance, and style. The style category generates many false positives.

The developers have started ignoring all the bot's comments, including the security ones, which are usually correct. What is the best strategy?
opcoes: Add a second model that reviews the first one's findings and discards those that look like false positives.
Temporarily turn off the style category, rewrite its criteria with what counts, what doesn't, and boundary examples, and turn it back on after measuring.
Add to the prompt "be conservative when flagging style issues".
Publish only the findings for which the model declares confidence above 90%.
questoes.explicacao: A noisy category erodes trust in the good ones. Turn it off, refine it with explicit criteria and boundary examples, and only then turn it back on.
feedbacks: More complex than necessary; the exam prefers explicit criteria before a second model to check the first.
Correct: restores trust immediately and fixes the cause with explicit criteria.
A vague instruction produces inconsistent results; "conservative" doesn't define what counts.
Self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated; it isn't a reliable filter.

questoes.pergunta:
In Orbital Logística's automated review, similar problems receive different severities in different PRs (the same empty `catch` becomes "low" in one PR and "high" in another).

Which prompt change tends to give more consistency?
opcoes: Instruct "use your good judgment as a senior engineer to define the severity".
Run the review three times and use the most frequent severity.
Include 2 to 4 examples of boundary cases, each with the snippet, the severity, and the reasoning.
Include 40 real examples of previous findings with their severities, to cover as many situations as possible.
questoes.explicacao: Few-shot with a few varied examples, each with its reasoning, teaches the criterion in a generalizable way. Combine it with explicit criteria per severity.
feedbacks: "Good judgment" is the opposite of an explicit criterion; it's the source of the inconsistency.
Voting reduces variance, but doesn't define the criterion; it triples the cost without fixing the cause.
Correct: examples with reasoning on ambiguous cases are the right use of few-shot.
Too many examples are expensive, encourage rote memorization, and tend to repeat the common cases instead of the boundaries.

questoes.pergunta:
Orbital Logística wants the CI review to follow exactly the same conventions the developers use locally with Claude Code (architecture, testing patterns, error handling).

What is the simplest and most sustainable way to ensure this?
opcoes: Keep the conventions in the project's `CLAUDE.md`, versioned in the repository; `claude -p` in the CI checkout loads the same file as the developers.
Copy the conventions into an `--append-system-prompt` in the CI workflow, ensuring the review always receives them, and keep them in sync with CLAUDE.md.
Create a `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` in the CI runner image with the conventions.
Paste the conventions into the job's prompt text on every run.
questoes.explicacao: CLI, IDE, and CI use the same engine: the project CLAUDE.md applies on every surface. A single source of truth avoids drift.
feedbacks: Correct: a single source, versioned alongside the code.
Duplicates the source of truth; the two copies will diverge. `--append-system-prompt` is for CI-specific instructions.
Lives outside the repository and diverges from what the developers use; it's the runner's user configuration, not the team's.
Same duplication, now in the workflow; manual maintenance that is prone to drift.

questoes.pergunta:
In Orbital Logística's CI, the review job needs instructions that only apply there: "don't propose fixes, only point out findings" and "ignore generated files in `/generated`".

How do you add these instructions without losing Claude Code's default behavior and without affecting the developers?
opcoes: Create a `SessionStart` hook that deletes the `/generated` folder before each session.
Pass the instructions with `--append-system-prompt` in the job's invocation.
Replace the entire system prompt with `--system-prompt` containing only these two rules.
Add the rules to the project's `CLAUDE.md`, so they also apply in CI.
questoes.explicacao: `--append-system-prompt` adds instructions to the default prompt without replacing it. CI-only rules stay in the CI invocation.
feedbacks: Deleting files from the checkout is an unnecessary side effect and doesn't address the rule about not proposing fixes.
Correct: adds what's needed while keeping the default behavior.
Replacing discards Claude Code's default instructions, which changes the agent's behavior in unexpected ways.
It would affect the developers locally, who often specifically want Claude to propose fixes.

questoes.pergunta:
Orbital Logística has auto-merge for dependency PRs. The policy says: never merge if Claude's review flags a critical-severity finding.

Today that rule lives only in the prompt ("if there is a critical finding, do not approve"), and a PR with a critical vulnerability was merged. How do you enforce the rule?
opcoes: Emit schema-validated JSON with each finding's severity and block the merge in a deterministic pipeline step if there is a critical finding.
Reinforce the prompt with capital letters and repeat the rule at the beginning and the end.
Give the agent permission to run `gh pr merge` and instruct it to merge only after checking, finding by finding, that none of them has critical severity.
Block the merge only when the model declares low confidence in its own analysis.
questoes.explicacao: A rule with security consequences belongs in deterministic code. The model produces structured data; the pipeline decides.
feedbacks: Correct: the critical decision moves out of the prompt and into a deterministic check.
Still probabilistic; prompt reinforcement reduces, but doesn't eliminate, the failure rate.
Puts the critical decision in the hands of the model, which is exactly what failed.
Self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated and has no relation to the presence of critical findings.

questoes.pergunta:
Orbital Logística's review runs four subagents in parallel (security, bugs, performance, tests) and a coordinator consolidates them. On a recent PR, the security subagent timed out.

The report posted on the PR said "Security: no findings". How should the system have behaved?
opcoes: The subagent tries to recover locally (retry with backoff); if the failure persists, it returns a structured error and the coordinator publishes the partial report marking security as "not analyzed" and the check as inconclusive.
The coordinator should have aborted the entire review and published nothing until all subagents completed.
The coordinator should have omitted the security section from the report, since there are no findings to show.
The subagent should have returned an empty list, but the coordinator should rerun the entire review next time.
questoes.explicacao: Failure ≠ empty. Recover transient errors locally; what can't be resolved is propagated with context, and the partial result goes ahead with the gap made explicit.
feedbacks: Correct: recovers what it can, propagates what it can't, and doesn't hide the gap.
Aborting everything because of one step wastes the valid findings of the other three subagents.
Omitting it hides the gap; the reader concludes that security was reviewed.
An empty list as success is the anti-pattern of silent error suppression.
